question: A 78-year-old patient with advanced dementia cannot self-report pain. Which validated tool is most appropriate to assess pain in this patient?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The NRS requires numerical comprehension and verbal self-report — not reliable in patients with advanced dementia.
The VAS requires the patient to mark a 10 cm line — this abstract task is not feasible in advanced dementia.

Correct. Observational tools such as the Abbey Pain Scale and PAINAD assess behavioural indicators (facial grimacing, vocalisation, body language, breathing pattern) without requiring self-report — validated specifically for dementia.
The McGill Pain Questionnaire requires verbal description of pain quality — not applicable in patients who cannot communicate reliably.

overallFeedback.feedback: In cognitively impaired or non-verbal patients, use behavioural observational tools (Abbey Pain Scale, PAINAD) rather than self-report scales (NRS, VAS, McGill).
Correct. Always match the pain assessment tool to the patient's communication capacity. Observational tools are mandatory for non-verbal and cognitively impaired patients.
